content: Zinc oxide is a chemical compound with the molecular formula ZnO. It is nearly insoluble in water but can dissolve in acids and alkalis. It naturally occurs as white hexagonal crystals or as a white powder, commonly referred to as zinc white. Notably, it retains its white color even when exposed to hydrogen sulfide or ultraviolet light. Crystalline zinc oxide exhibits piezoelectric properties and is thermochromic, meaning it changes color from white to yellow when heated and reverts to white upon cooling. At approximately 1975 °C, zinc oxide decomposes into zinc vapor and oxygen. High-quality single-crystalline zinc oxide is nearly transparent. In nature, it is found as the mineral zincite. Medical Applications Zinc oxide lozenges are widely available as over-the-counter remedies for the common cold, but clinical studies have not demonstrated significant efficacy. When combined with approximately 0.5% iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃), it forms calamine, which is a key ingredient in calamine lotion. Historically, the minerals zincite and hemimorphite were also referred to as calamine. In dentistry, zinc oxide mixed with eugenol forms zinc oxide eugenol, which is used in restorative and prosthodontic applications. Additionally, zinc peroxide (ZnO₂·½H₂O), a white to yellow powder, is utilized in antiseptic ointments. As a Pigment Zinc oxide, known as zinc white, is used as a pigment in paints. It is more opaque than lithopone but less opaque than titanium dioxide. It is also employed in paper coatings. A specialized grade of zinc white, called Chinese white, is used in artists' pigments. Due to its ability to absorb both UVA and UVB rays, zinc oxide is a key ingredient in sunscreens, ointments, creams, and lotions, providing protection against sunburn and ultraviolet-induced skin damage. It is the broadest-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber approved by the FDA for use in sunscreens and is completely photostable. Furthermore, zinc oxide exhibits antimicrobial and antifungal properties, making it the primary active ingredient recommended by pediatricians for treating diaper rash. Rubber Manufacturing Zinc oxide, in combination with stearic acid, is used in the commercial production of rubber products. This mixture facilitates a faster and more controlled curing process for rubber. Zinc oxide also serves as a filler in certain rubber formulations. Electronic Materials Zinc oxide is a semiconductor with a direct bandgap energy of 3.37 eV at room temperature. It is commonly used in laser diodes and light-emitting diodes (LEDs) due to its exciton and biexciton energies of 60 meV and 15 meV, respectively. These properties are expected to improve further with epitaxial growth techniques. N-type doping of zinc oxide is achieved by introducing elements such as aluminum, indium, or excess zinc, which increase conductivity by creating oxygen vacancies. P-type doping, however, remains challenging and is an area of active research, with arsenic being a leading candidate dopant. Zinc oxide is used in thin-film solar cells, liquid crystal displays (LCDs), and flat-panel displays. When appropriately doped, it can be both transparent and conductive, making it suitable for use as a transparent electrode. Indium tin oxide (ITO) is another transparent conducting oxide often used in microelectronics. Zinc oxide has also been investigated for spintronics applications due to theoretical predictions of room-temperature ferromagnetism, although reports of ferromagnetism remain unsubstantiated. Zinc oxide layers are typically deposited using sputter deposition or chemical vapor deposition (CVD). The latter method produces rough layers that scatter incoming light, enhancing the efficiency of solar cells. Zinc oxide can also act as a chemical reagent in Friedel-Crafts acylation reactions. Pyroelectric Coefficients Primary pyroelectric coefficient: -6.8 µC/m²·K Secondary pyroelectric coefficient: -2.5 µC/m²·K Total pyroelectric coefficient: -9.4 µC/m²·K Production Methods Zinc oxide is primarily produced through two processes: French Process In the French process, metallic zinc is melted in a graphite crucible and vaporized at temperatures above 907 °C. The zinc vapor reacts instantaneously with oxygen in the air to form zinc oxide, accompanied by a temperature drop and bright luminescence. The resulting zinc oxide particles are transported into a cooling duct and collected in a bag house. This indirect method, popularized by LeClaire in France in 1844, produces zinc oxide particles with sizes ranging from 0.1 micrometers to a few micrometers. The French process accounts for the majority of the world's zinc oxide production, which is used in industries such as rubber, varistors, sunscreens, paints, healthcare, and poultry nutrition. Recent advancements include the synthesis of acicular nanostructures (e.g., rods, wires, tripods, tetrapods, plates) using a modified French process called the catalyst-free combust-oxidized mesh (CFCOM) process. These nanostructures typically have micrometer-length rods with diameters below 100 nanometers. A related direct method involves reducing zinc ores or roasted sulfide concentrates with coal in a furnace, followed by the reaction of vaporized zinc with oxygen to form zinc oxide. American Process In the American process, zinc ore (zinc ash) is dissolved as zinc chloride (ZnCl₂) and precipitated with an alkali. The resulting zinc oxide is referred to as Active Zinc Oxide. Safety Zinc oxide fumes are generated during the melting of brass, as the melting point of brass is close to the boiling point of zinc. Inhalation of zinc oxide fumes, such as during welding, can lead to a condition known as metal fume fever, a temporary illness affecting the nervous system.
